alabama.enforce_note: Non-competes are void by default under Ala. Code § 8-1-190(a) unless they fit a narrow statutory exception and protect a defined protectable interest.
alabama.state_note: An employee non-compete of two years or less is presumed reasonable, and the worker must already be employed when the agreement is signed.
alabama.threshold_note: Alabama has no earnings threshold; instead, non-competes are unenforceable against professionals such as physicians and attorneys and against independent contractors.

alaska.enforce_note: Alaska has no non-compete statute; courts enforce non-competes only if they are reasonable in time, area, and scope and protect a legitimate business interest.
alaska.state_note: Alaska courts view non-competes with disfavor and construe them strictly against the employer, and may narrow an overbroad agreement drafted in good faith instead of voiding it.
alaska.threshold_note: Alaska has no earnings threshold, so a non-compete can in theory apply at any pay level if it passes the reasonableness test.

arizona.enforce_note: Arizona courts enforce non-competes only if they are no broader than needed to protect a legitimate business interest and are reasonable in time, area, and scope.
arizona.state_note: Under A.R.S. § 23-494, radio and television employers may not require a non-compete as a condition of employment, and courts use a strict blue-pencil rule that only strikes severable parts.
arizona.threshold_note: Arizona has no general earnings threshold; the only statutory ban covers broadcast employees.

arkansas.enforce_note: Arkansas enforces a non-compete only if it is ancillary to employment, protects a defined protectable business interest, and is limited in time and scope to no more than necessary.
arkansas.state_note: A post-termination restriction of two years is presumptively reasonable, and for agreements signed after July 21, 2015 a court must narrow an unreasonable covenant rather than void it outright.
arkansas.threshold_note: Arkansas has no earnings threshold; the statute instead limits enforcement to agreements protecting trade secrets, customer lists, goodwill, confidential information, and similar interests.

california.enforce_note: California voids every contract restraining a person from a lawful profession, trade, or business, including any employment non-compete no matter how narrowly tailored, except for narrow sale-of-business exceptions.
california.legal_aid_name: Legal Aid Foundation of Los Angeles
california.state_note: Since January 1, 2024, it is unlawful to include or try to enforce a void non-compete, and an employer that does so commits a civil violation with a private right of action.
california.statute_name: Business and Professions Code, Chapter 1, Contracts in Restraint of Trade
california.threshold_note: The ban covers all employees at every pay level, with no earnings threshold to meet.

colorado.enforce_note: Colorado voids non-competes by default and enforces one only against a highly compensated worker, only to protect trade secrets, and only with the required advance written notice.
colorado.state_note: An employer that presents or tries to enforce a void covenant faces actual damages plus a $5,000 penalty per affected worker, and since August 6, 2025 physicians, physician assistants, APRNs, certified midwives, and dentists cannot be bound at any pay level.
colorado.statute_name: Unlawful to Intimidate Worker — Agreement Not to Compete
colorado.threshold_note: For 2026 the highly compensated worker threshold is $130,014 in annualized cash compensation, met both when the agreement is signed and when it is enforced, and it adjusts annually.

connecticut.enforce_note: Connecticut has no general non-compete statute, so courts enforce a non-compete only if it is reasonable in time, area, fairness to the employer, effect on the worker, and effect on the public.
connecticut.state_note: Separate statutes void or limit non-competes for specific jobs, including physicians (one year and 15 miles), security guards, broadcast employees, and homemakers and home health workers.
connecticut.threshold_note: Connecticut has no general earnings threshold; proposed bills in 2023 and 2025 that would have set one at three times the minimum wage were not enacted.

delaware.enforce_note: Delaware has no general non-compete statute, so courts enforce a non-compete only if it is reasonable in duration and area, advances a legitimate economic interest, and balances in the employer's favor.
delaware.state_note: Under 6 Del. C. § 2707 a physician's non-compete is void, although the agreement may still require damages reasonably related to the injury from leaving, and Delaware courts will not rewrite an overbroad covenant.
delaware.threshold_note: Delaware has no earnings threshold; the only statutory rule voids physician non-competes.

florida.enforce_note: Florida enforces a non-compete that is in writing, signed by the worker, protects a listed legitimate business interest, and is reasonable in time, area, and line of business.
florida.state_note: A restraint of six months or less is presumed reasonable for a former employee and more than two years is presumed unreasonable, and a court must narrow an overbroad restraint rather than void it.
florida.statute_name: Valid Restraints of Trade or Commerce
florida.threshold_note: Florida has no general earnings threshold; the 2025 CHOICE Act's higher-pay test only governs its optional four-year, per se enforceable agreements, with the pay line varying by county at over twice the county mean wage.

georgia.enforce_note: Georgia enforces a non-compete only under the Georgia Restrictive Covenants Act, only against workers in four covered job categories, and only if it is reasonable in time, area, and scope.
georgia.state_note: For a former employee, a restraint of two years or less is presumed reasonable and more than two years is presumed unreasonable, and a court may narrow an overbroad covenant instead of voiding it.
georgia.threshold_note: Georgia has no salary threshold; the gate is job function, so ordinary workers outside the four categories in O.C.G.A. § 13-8-53(a) cannot be bound.
